children.title: Dual-Certificate Tightening Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where available dual certificates support reliable variable-domain reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Certificate Tightening Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions distinguishing validity from exact recovery of auxiliary coordinate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an auxiliary minimization problem with value \(p^*\), a dual-feasible point with objective \(d\) always certifies \(d\le p^*\) under weak duality. It certifies the exact coordinate bound precisely when \(d=p^*\). In a convex formulation, feasibility, closed proper convex data, and a Slater point are sufficient for zero duality gap and dual attainment under the standard finite-dimensional constraint qualification. In a nonconvex formulation, dual feasibility still gives a valid bound, but equality with \(p^*\) requires a separate zero-gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility guarantees safe tightening; exact tightening additionally requires zero duality gap, supplied in convex cases by suitable constraint qualifications.
assumptions_latex: The auxiliary primal and dual obey weak duality.
For the sufficient exactness regime, the auxiliary problem is finite-dimensional and convex with a Slater point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\le p^*\), and the dual certificate is exact if and only if \(d=p^*\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Weak-duality validity is correct, but the stated Slater regime is too compressed to guarantee both zero gap and dual attainment without explicitly specifying finite optimal value, domains, equality constraints, and the applicable relative-interior constraint qualification. The cited section must be inspected to determine the correct version.

children.title: Tightening Reliability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Numerical or relaxation-quality conditions limiting certificate-based bound reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Tightening Reliability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure modes that make purported dual or Lagrangian tightening unsafe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed lower update \(x_i\ge b\\) is reliable only when \(b\le\inf_{x\in R}x_i\) for a set \(R\supseteq F\); the analogous upper update requires \(b\ge\sup_{x\in R}x_i\). A local stationary value of a nonconvex auxiliary problem, a dual vector violating its sign or cone constraints, or an uncertified numerical objective need not satisfy these inequalities. Using such a value can delete feasible points. Infeasibility may be concluded only from a valid infeasibility certificate, not merely from failure of a local solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local solutions, dual-infeasible multipliers, and uncertified numerical values cannot safely tighten bounds or establish node infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the node-feasible set and \(R\) is the set used for certification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reliability requires \(F\subseteq R\) and certified global inequalities in the safe direction.

notation.meaning: certifying relaxation or auxiliary feasible region

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but no source is supplied for the specialized reliability claims. In addition, the inline expression for the lower update contains an erroneous LaTeX line-break command after b and must be repaired when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.top_down_role: Structural regimes in which a quadratic relaxation closes its relevant projection or optimization gap.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\) with finite nondegenerate bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick convex hull for one bounded bilinear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite bounds \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\), the convex hull of \(S=\{(x,y,w):\ell_x\le x\le u_x,\ \ell_y\le y\le u_y,\ w=xy\}\) is exactly the polytope defined by the box bounds and \[w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\quad w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\] \[w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\quad w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y.\] Thus the four McCormick inequalities introduce no convex-hull gap for a single bounded product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The four McCormick inequalities exactly describe the convex hull of one bilinear equality over a rectangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Product Hull Exactness
Indicator-Quadratic Hull Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective hull of an on/off convex quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) and \(S=\{(0,0,t):t\ge0\}\cup\{(1,x,t):t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx\}\). Its closed convex hull is \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(z,x,t):0\le z\le1,\ t\ge0,\ x^{\mathsf T}Qx\le tz\}.\] Equivalently, for \(z>0\) the defining inequality is \(t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx/z\), while at \(z=0\) positive-semidefiniteness forces \(Q^{1/2}x=0\). If \(Q\succ0\), this forces \(x=0\), matching the off state exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective inequality gives the closed convex hull of an on/off positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph; positive definiteness enforces zero activity when off.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix.
The indicator set has no additional bounds or constraints on \(x\).

notation.meaning: on/off indicator, relaxed in the hull

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Recovery Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori exactness certificate for a lifted semidefinite relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a QCQP lifted with variables \((x,X)\), where each quadratic form is linearized by replacing \(xx^{\mathsf T}\) with \(X\), and impose \(Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\). If an optimal relaxed solution \((x^*,X^*)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(Y^*)=1\), then \(X^*=x^*(x^*)^{\mathsf T}\). Consequently every lifted quadratic constraint and objective equals its original QCQP counterpart at \(x^*\); if required integer coordinates of \(x^*\) are integral, \(x^*\) is globally optimal and the relaxation is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal rank-one lifted matrix recovers the original quadratic products; with required integrality, it certifies global exactness.
assumptions_latex: The semidefinite model is a valid relaxation of the QCQP.
\((x^*,X^*)\) is globally optimal for that relaxation.
All required discrete coordinates of \(x^*\) are integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(Y^*)=1\Rightarrow X^*=x^*(x^*)^{\mathsf T}\) and the relaxation value equals the QCQP optimum.

notation.meaning: lift of the quadratic product matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-one condition has the correct certificate role and the stated implication is standard, but the record has no source for the lifted SDP recovery and mixed-integer exactness claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Constraint Exactness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A three-variable QCQP showing failure of rank-relaxation exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{x_1x_2+x_1x_3+x_2x_3:x_i^2=1,\ i=1,2,3\}\). Every feasible sign vector has objective at least \(-1\), and this value is attained. Its standard semidefinite relaxation minimizes \(X_{12}+X_{13}+X_{23}\) subject to \(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{ii}=1\). The Gram matrix of three unit vectors separated pairwise by \(120\) degrees is feasible and has every off-diagonal entry equal to \(-1/2\), giving value \(-3/2\). Hence the relaxation has a strict gap and no rank-one optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three quadratic equality constraints admit an SDP value of minus three halves while the original sign problem has optimum minus one.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation drops the nonconvex condition \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\) while retaining \(X\succeq0\) and unit diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-3/2\le v_{\mathrm{SDP}}<v_{\mathrm{QCQP}}=-1\).

notation.meaning: semidefinite lift of the pairwise products

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied. Moreover, feasibility of the 120-degree Gram matrix proves \(v_{\mathrm{SDP}}\le-3/2\), whereas the conclusion states the reverse inequality. A complete treatment should establish the matching lower bound and state \(v_{\mathrm{SDP}}=-3/2<v_{\mathrm{QCQP}}=-1\).

children.title: Global-Search Certificate Families
children.top_down_role: Certificates tied specifically to global mixed-integer quadratic search.

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Node Lower-Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable lower bounds used to prune minimization nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a branch-and-bound node let \(F_N\) be the node-feasible set and let \(R_N\supseteq F_N\). A valid lower-bound certificate consists of a function \(\underline f\) satisfying \(\underline f(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F_N\), together with a verifiable scalar \(\beta_N\) satisfying \(\beta_N\le\inf_{x\in R_N}\underline f(x)\). Then \(\beta_N\le\inf_{x\in F_N}f(x)\). For minimization, the node may be pruned by bound whenever \(\beta_N\) is no smaller than the incumbent objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified underestimator minimized over a superset of the node-feasible set yields a valid node lower bound and a pruning test.
assumptions_latex: \(F_N\subseteq R_N\).
\(\underline f(x)\le f(x)\) on \(F_N\).
\(\beta_N\) is a verified lower bound for the relaxed underestimator problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta_N\le\inf_{x\in F_N}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Exactness Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori certificate equating relaxation and original optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\) and relaxation \(R\supseteq F\), let \(L\) be a certified relaxation optimum and let \(x^*\in F\) be recoverable from an optimal relaxed solution. If the relaxed and original objectives agree at that solution, so that \(L=f(x^*)\), then \(L\le v_F\le f(x^*)=L\). Thus \(v_F=L\), \(x^*\) is globally optimal, and the relaxation is exact. Lift consistency, rank-one structure, and required integrality are verifiable mechanisms for establishing recoverability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible recovered point whose objective equals a certified relaxation bound proves global optimality and relaxation exactness.
assumptions_latex: \(R\supseteq F\) and \(L\) is a certified lower bound attained by the relaxation.
\(x^*\in F\) is recovered from an optimal relaxed solution.

notation.meaning: original feasible set and its relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical certificate is standard and fits the container, but the locator 'Part II Global Optimization' has no section, theorem, definition, or page and therefore fails the citation-specificity requirement. A precise locator supporting relaxation-bound equality and feasible recovery is required.

children.title: Spatial Exhaustion Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates based on complete or sufficiently refined coverage of the relevant spatial domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Exhaustion Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite spatial branch-and-bound certificate for a minimization MIQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be covered by finitely many terminal regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\), and let \(J=\{j:F\cap R_j\ne\varnothing\}\). For every \(j\in J\), provide a valid lower bound \(L_j\le\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap R_j\}\); for every \(j\notin J\), provide a verifiable infeasibility certificate. Also provide a feasible incumbent \(\hat x\in F\) with \(U=f(\hat x)\). If every generated region is represented by terminal descendants or is validly fathomed, then \(\underline L=\min_{j\in J}L_j\le f^*\le U\). If \(L_j\ge U\) for every \(j\in J\), then \(f(\hat x)=f^*\), so \(\hat x\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite terminal cover, certified infeasibility for empty regions, valid lower bounds for nonempty regions, and a feasible incumbent give global bounds. The incumbent is globally optimal when every nonempty terminal region has lower bound at least its value.
assumptions_latex: The minimization problem has a nonempty feasible set \(F\) and finite optimum \(f^*\).
Every regional lower bound is valid on its associated nonempty region.
The terminal regions cover \(F\), and every asserted empty region has a verifiable infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\underline L\le f^*\le U\), and \(L_j\ge U\) for every \(j\in J\) certifies global optimality of \(\hat x\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the mixed-integer quadratic problem.
Indices of terminal regions having nonempty intersection with the feasible set.
Valid lower bound on the objective over terminal region \(j\).
Objective value of the feasible incumbent \(\hat x\).

children.top_down_role: Certificates based on the separation between valid global bounds.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with finite optimum \(f^*\).
The reported lower and upper bounds are globally valid.
The requested tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies \(f(\hat x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and relative gap certificates for finite-valued minimization MIQPs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(L\le f^*\le U=f(\hat x)\) for a feasible point \(\hat x\). The tuple \((\hat x,L,U)\) is an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate if \(U-L\le\varepsilon\), because then \(0\le f(\hat x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\). For a prescribed scale \(s>0\), it is a relative \(\varepsilon\)-certificate if \((U-L)/\max\{s,|U|,|L|\}\le\varepsilon\). The scale convention must be recorded; without it, a claimed relative gap is not uniquely defined near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent and a valid global lower bound certify absolute optimality error by their difference; relative certification additionally requires an explicit positive scaling convention.

children.title: Certificate Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Search regimes where spatial coverage evidence supports or complements gap certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for combining spatial and gap certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Certificates \(C_1,\ldots,C_r\) are compatible when they concern the same original feasible set \(F\), minimization objective \(f\), objective sense, and normalization; every reported lower bound \(L_k\) is certified to satisfy \(L_k\le f^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\}\), and every reported upper bound \(U_k\) is the value \(f(x_k)\) of a point \(x_k\in F\). Under these conditions, \(L=\max_{1\le k\le r}L_k\) and \(U=\min_{1\le k\le r}U_k\) satisfy \(L\le f^*\le U\). A bound derived from a relaxation or transformed objective is compatible precisely when a valid translation certifies the corresponding bound for \(f\) on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificates can be combined when all their bounds are valid for the same original minimization objective and feasible set. The largest certified lower bound and smallest feasible upper bound then remain valid; relaxation bounds are allowed when their validity for the original problem is established.
assumptions_latex: All component certificates concern the same original optimization instance and objective sense.
Every bound is expressed in, or validly translated into, the same objective normalization.
Every claimed feasible point satisfies the original mixed-integer constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatible certificates imply \(L\le f^*\le U\), where \(L=\max_{1\le k\le r}L_k\) and \(U=\min_{1\le k\le r}U_k\).

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound supplied by certificate \(k\).

assumptions_latex: Input coefficients are rational and encoded in binary.
The number of binary variables is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact convex MIQP optimization is NP-hard, even when \(Q=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case hardness caused solely by integrality in convex MIQP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider rational instances \(\min\{\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\) with \(Q\succeq0\). This class is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions: setting \(Q=0\) leaves rational zero-one linear optimization as a subclass. Consequently, convexity of the continuous objective does not yield polynomial-time solvability when the discrete dimension is variable. The hardness assertion concerns exact global optimization in the binary encoding model and does not assert hardness when the integer dimension is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity does not remove combinatorial hardness: convex MIQP contains zero-one linear optimization by setting its positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Hardness in Convex MIQP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction from zero-one linear optimization is mathematically plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits, but no source or inspectable reduction locator supports the NP-hardness claim.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimization search region can be discarded when its valid lower bound is no better than a valid attainable upper bound from another region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2\subseteq X\), and suppose \(\underline f_1\leq \min_{x\in Y_1}f(x)\) and \(\overline f_2\geq \min_{x\in Y_2}f(x)\), where \(\overline f_2\) is the value of an attainable solution in \(Y_2\). If \(\overline f_2\leq \underline f_1\), then no point in \(Y_1\) has objective value smaller than the attainable value \(\overline f_2\), so \(Y_1\) may be pruned without losing a better solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a valid lower bound for one search region is at least an attainable objective value from another region, the first region cannot contain a better solution and may be pruned.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core OPEN-list iteration with lower-bound pruning and incumbent improvement; optimality at termination relies on the standard exhaustive-partition and valid-bound invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an incumbent feasible point \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\) with \(\mathrm{UPPER}=f(x^{\mathrm{inc}})\) and an OPEN collection of search regions. Remove \(Y\in\mathrm{OPEN}\); for every child \(Y_j\), compute a valid lower bound \(\underline f_{Y_j}\leq\inf_{x\in Y_j}f(x)\) and, when available, a feasible candidate \(\bar x_j\in Y_j\). Retain \(Y_j\) in OPEN only if \(\underline f_{Y_j}<\mathrm{UPPER}\). If \(f(\bar x_j)<\mathrm{UPPER}\), set \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}=\bar x_j\) and \(\mathrm{UPPER}=f(\bar x_j)\). Repeat while OPEN is nonempty. If the children exhaustively partition every expanded region, all discarded regions satisfy their valid pruning tests, and the finite search terminates with \(\mathrm{OPEN}=\varnothing\), then \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly expand an open search region, retain only children whose valid lower bounds can beat the incumbent, and update the incumbent whenever a better feasible point is found. Under exhaustive branching, valid bounds, and finite termination, an empty OPEN list certifies that the incumbent is optimal.

assumptions_latex: Weighted MAX-CUT instances have nonnegative rational edge weights.
The number of binary variables is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary quadratic minimization remains NP-hard with an indefinite objective matrix.

notation.meaning: Graph Laplacian of a weighted graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong nonconvexity does not become tractable merely because variables are binary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a weighted graph \(G\), a cut represented by \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) has weight \(x^{\mathsf T}L_Gx\). Hence MAX-CUT is equivalent to minimizing \(-x^{\mathsf T}L_Gx\) over binary \(x\). Introduce a continuous variable \(t\) constrained by \(t=0\) and add \(t^2\) to the objective. For any graph with a positive-weight edge, the resulting quadratic matrix has both a negative and a positive eigenvalue, while feasible objective values are unchanged. Thus exact binary quadratic minimization with an indefinite matrix is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MAX-CUT yields a nonconvex binary quadratic objective; adding a positive quadratic term in a variable fixed to zero makes the matrix genuinely indefinite without changing the problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Quadratic Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The MAX-CUT construction and fixed-zero auxiliary variable produce the claimed indefinite matrix, but the NP-hardness assertion has no cited authoritative source or reduction locator.

assumptions_latex: The total decision dimension \(n\), or the designated integer dimension \(p\), is treated as a constant.
All numerical data are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complexity claims for the regime measure growth in encoding length while the selected dimension parameter remains constant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter convention distinguishing fixed total dimension from fixed integer dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of MIQP instances is in a fixed-total-dimension regime when there exists a constant \(n_0\), independent of input length \(N\), such that every instance has \(n\le n_0\). It is in a fixed-integer-dimension regime when only \(p\le p_0\) is constant, while the number of continuous variables may grow with \(N\). These regimes are distinct. A running time of the form \(g(n)N^c\), respectively \(g(p)N^c\), is polynomial within the corresponding fixed-dimension regime when \(c\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-dimension statement must specify whether total or only integer dimension is constant; polynomial complexity then refers to growth in the remaining binary input length.

children.title: Bounded-Domain Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior under finite or explicitly bounded variable domains.

assumptions_latex: Every integer variable has finite integral lower and upper bounds.
The continuous feasible region associated with each integer assignment is compact or otherwise attains its infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The discrete search set is finite with cardinality at most \(\prod_{i=1}^p(u_i-\ell_i+1)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain property, separated from polynomial-time tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(z_i\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\ell_i\le z_i\le u_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), then the set of possible integer vectors has cardinality at most \(M=\prod_{i=1}^p(u_i-\ell_i+1)\). Thus an exact method may enumerate all integer assignments and solve the resulting continuous quadratic subproblem for each assignment whenever those subproblems are globally solvable. Boundedness alone does not make this enumeration polynomial in the binary input length: \(M\) can be exponential when \(p\) grows or when binary-encoded bound widths grow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite integer bounds permit exhaustive enumeration, but the number of assignments can still be exponential in dimension or in the binary encoding of the bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Regimes

children.title: Dimension–Domain Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes shaped jointly by dimension restrictions and domain bounds.

assumptions_latex: There are \(p\) integer variables with domain sizes \(d_1,\ldots,d_p\).
Each fixed-integer continuous subproblem is solvable in time \(T(N)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enumeration requires at most \(\bigl(\prod_{i=1}^p d_i\bigr)T(N)\) subproblem time, up to polynomial bookkeeping.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration bound exposing the joint effect of dimension and domain cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let integer coordinate \(i\) have a finite domain of size \(d_i\). Exhaustive assignment generates at most \(M=\prod_{i=1}^p d_i\) continuous quadratic subproblems, so its running time is \(O(MT(N)+\operatorname{poly}(N,M))\). This is polynomial in \(N\) if \(p\) is fixed, every \(d_i\) is polynomially bounded in \(N\), and \(T(N)\) is polynomial. Fixing only \(p\) is insufficient for this enumeration argument when binary-encoded domains have exponentially many values; bounding only each \(d_i\) is insufficient when \(p\) grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration is polynomial only when the product of integer-domain sizes and the cost of each continuous subproblem are polynomial in input length.

assumptions_latex: Every variable has a finite domain of size at most \(D\).
The objective and constraints decompose into local factors whose primal interaction graph has treewidth \(w\).
A width-\(w\) tree decomposition is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dynamic programming solves the finite-domain problem in \(O(\operatorname{poly}(N)D^{w+1})\) time under the stated factorization.

notation.meaning: Treewidth of the primal interaction graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain factor-graph regime; sparsity must include constraints, not only the quadratic matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the primal interaction graph by joining two variables whenever they occur together in one quadratic term or constraint factor. If all variable domains have size at most \(D\), all factors are evaluable in polynomial time, and a tree decomposition of width \(w\) is given, dynamic programming over its bags stores at most \(D^{w+1}\) assignments per bag. The optimum is therefore computable in \(O(\operatorname{poly}(N)D^{w+1})\) time. Sparsity of the objective matrix alone gives no such bound when constraints create a dense interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded treewidth supports dynamic programming for finite-domain MIQP only when both objective and constraints respect the same sparse interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Interaction-Graph Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain tree-decomposition dynamic program is plausible and appropriately excludes continuous-domain extensions, but the exact complexity bound requires an authoritative source with a theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_C(x)=f(x)+C\). The objectives \(f\) and \(f_C\) have identical feasible minimizers, but the multiplicative quotient \(f_C(\hat x)/f_C^*=(f(\hat x)+C)/(f^*+C)\) varies with \(C\) and is undefined when \(f^*+C=0\). Therefore a ratio guarantee requires an explicit sign and normalization condition, such as \(f^*>0\). An additive guarantee \(f(\hat x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) is shift-invariant, although its meaning still depends on objective scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative guarantees fail without positive normalization because an objective shift preserves minimizers but changes or destroys the ratio; additive error is shift-invariant.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Curvature Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic curvature classification for a quadratic objective on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) with a symmetric rational matrix \(Q\). Determine the signs of the eigenvalues of \(Q\), equivalently its inertia. Output that \(q\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\) exactly when \(Q\succeq0\), strictly convex exactly when \(Q\succ0\), concave exactly when \(Q\preceq0\), and strictly concave exactly when \(Q\prec0\). If \(Q\) has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue, output that \(q\) is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify the curvature of a quadratic on the full Euclidean space from the eigenvalue signs of its symmetric Hessian: positive semidefinite is convex, positive definite strictly convex, negative semidefinite concave, negative definite strictly concave, and mixed signs neither convex nor concave.
assumptions_latex: The objective is \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) with symmetric rational \(Q\).
Curvature is classified on the full space \(\mathbb R^n\).
Matrix-sign decisions are performed in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output gives the convexity or concavity class of \(q\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) from the definiteness or indefiniteness of \(Q\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric Hessian matrix of the quadratic objective.

children.title: Matrix Inertia Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of positive, negative, and zero spectral directions in quadratic matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Inertia Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric-factorization algorithm for detecting matrix inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a symmetric matrix \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Compute a symmetric pivoted factorization \(P^{\mathsf T}QP=LDL^{\mathsf T}\), where \(P\) is a permutation, \(L\) is nonsingular unit lower triangular, and \(D\) is block diagonal with blocks of order one or two. Count the positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of the blocks of \(D\), obtaining \((n_+,n_-,n_0)\). These counts are the inertia of \(Q\). Classify \(Q\) as positive definite when \((n_+,n_-,n_0)=(n,0,0)\), positive semidefinite when \(n_-=0\), negative definite when \((n_+,n_-,n_0)=(0,n,0)\), negative semidefinite when \(n_+=0\), and indefinite when \(n_+>0\) and \(n_->0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric pivoted LDL factorization reduces inertia detection to counting positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of its one-by-one and two-by-two diagonal blocks; the resulting counts determine definiteness, semidefiniteness, or indefiniteness.
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric.
The factorization and sign counts are exact, or numerical decisions are accompanied by certified error bounds sufficient to determine every sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block sign counts \((n_+,n_-,n_0)\) equal the inertia of \(Q\) and determine its definiteness classification.

notation.meaning: Permutation matrix used by the symmetric pivoted factorization.
Block diagonal factor with blocks of order one or two.
Counts of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic forms, definiteness, and principal minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for real quadratic forms and symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), a quadratic form is \(f(x)=x^\top Qx\). With \(Q_0=(Q+Q^\top)/2\), one has \(x^\top Qx=x^\top Q_0x\) for every \(x\), so \(Q\) may be assumed symmetric. For symmetric \(Q\), the form is positive definite if \(x^\top Qx>0\) for every \(x\ne0\), positive semidefinite if \(x^\top Qx\ge0\) for every \(x\), negative definite if \(x^\top Qx<0\) for every \(x\ne0\), and negative semidefinite if \(x^\top Qx\le0\) for every \(x\). Its principal minors are \(\det Q[I,I]\) for nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\); its leading principal minors are \(\Delta_k=\det Q[1{:}k,1{:}k]\), \(k=1,\ldots,n\), with \(\Delta_n=\det Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real quadratic form is x transpose Q x and depends only on the symmetric part of Q. Positive and negative definite or semidefinite forms are classified by the sign of this value for all vectors, with strict inequalities restricted to nonzero vectors. Principal minors are determinants of principal submatrices, and leading principal minors use the first k rows and columns.
assumptions_latex: Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}
x\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\top Qx=x^\top\!\left(\frac{Q+Q^\top}{2}\right)x\quad\text{for all }x,\quad \Delta_k=\det Q[1{:}k,1{:}k].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix inertia, signature, and congruence invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral definition of inertia together with Sylvester invariance and LDL-based recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric A, let \mathcal I(A)=(n_-,n_0,n_+), where n_-,n_0,n_+ count its negative, zero, and positive eigenvalues. Its signature is n_+-n_- and \operatorname{rank}A=n_++n_-. A positive definite n\times n matrix has inertia (0,0,n), while a positive semidefinite one has inertia (0,k,n-k) for some k\geq0. For every nonsingular T, \mathcal I(TAT^T)=\mathcal I(A). Consequently, if A=LDL^T with L nonsingular, then \mathcal I(A)=\mathcal I(D).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inertia of a symmetric matrix counts its negative, zero, and positive eigenvalues; its signature is the positive count minus the negative count, and its rank is the sum of those counts. Inertia is invariant under nonsingular congruence, so it can be recovered from the diagonal factor in an LDL transpose factorization.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathcal S^n
T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\text{ nonsingular}
A=LDL^T\text{ with }L\text{ nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal I(A)=(n_-,n_0,n_+),\quad \operatorname{sig}(A)=n_+-n_-,\quad \operatorname{rank}A=n_++n_-,\quad \mathcal I(TAT^T)=\mathcal I(A),\quad \mathcal I(A)=\mathcal I(D).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity and spectral classification of a symmetric quadratic function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete algebraic and curvature classification for an unconstrained symmetric quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi(x)=c^Tx+\tfrac12x^TGx\) with \(G=G^T\), \(\Phi(\widehat x+\alpha p)=\Phi(\widehat x)+\alpha p^T(G\widehat x+c)+\tfrac12\alpha^2p^TGp\). A stationary point exists exactly when \(Gx^*=-c\) is compatible, and it is unique when \(G\) is nonsingular. If the system is incompatible, \(\Phi\) is unbounded above and below. At a stationary point, \(\Phi(x^*+\alpha p)=\Phi(x^*)+\tfrac12\alpha^2p^TGp\); hence \(G\succ0\) gives a unique global minimum, \(G\succeq0\) gives a weak local minimum whenever a stationary point exists, and an indefinite nonsingular \(G\) gives a saddle point with \(\Phi\) unbounded above and below. Along an eigenvector \(u_j\), the change is \(\tfrac12\alpha^2\lambda_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric quadratic has stationary points exactly when its linear term lies in the range of its Hessian. Its behavior at such points is determined by the Hessian eigenvalues: positive definite gives a unique global minimum, positive semidefinite gives flat minimum directions, and indefinite nonsingular curvature gives a saddle and two-sided unboundedness. Incompatibility of the stationarity equations also makes the quadratic unbounded above and below.
assumptions_latex: \Phi(x)=c^Tx+\frac12x^TGx
c\in\mathbb{R}^n
G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
G=G^T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla\Phi(x^*)=0\iff Gx^*=-c;\quad \Phi(x^*+\alpha p)-\Phi(x^*)=\frac12\alpha^2p^TGp,\ \text{with the stated compatibility and inertia classification}

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Singular Classification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical inertia classification of a symmetric quadratic matrix under bounded eigenvalue error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), and suppose computed eigenvalues \(\widehat\lambda_i\) satisfy \(|\widehat\lambda_i-\lambda_i(Q)|\leq\eta\). A sign is certified only when its interval \([\widehat\lambda_i-\eta,\widehat\lambda_i+\eta]\) excludes zero. If an interval contains zero, the corresponding positive, negative, or zero classification is not certified. In particular, when \(|\lambda_i(Q)|<\eta\), symmetric perturbations \(E\) with \(\|E\|_2\leq\eta\) can move that eigenvalue across zero, so the inertia and curvature class are unstable at the tolerance scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An eigenvalue whose error interval crosses zero has no certified sign; perturbations within the error tolerance can change the reported inertia and curvature class.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\)
\(|\widehat\lambda_i-\lambda_i(Q)|\leq\eta\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in[\widehat\lambda_i-\eta,\widehat\lambda_i+\eta]\Rightarrow\operatorname{sign}(\lambda_i(Q))\text{ is uncertified}\).

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Product Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-based detection under the symmetric convention \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx+d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), write \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx+d\). Distinct variables \(x_i\) and \(x_j\) form a quadratic product precisely when \(Q_{ij}\neq0\), because their expanded coefficient is \(Q_{ij}x_ix_j\). A square term in \(x_i\) is present precisely when \(Q_{ii}\neq0\), with coefficient \(\tfrac12Q_{ii}x_i^2\). Thus the off-diagonal support of \(Q\) detects bilinear products, while its diagonal support detects squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the symmetric half-quadratic convention, nonzero off-diagonal entries detect cross-products and nonzero diagonal entries detect squared variables.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\)
\(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx+d\)

notation.meaning: indices of nonzero entries of Q

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Rank-Structure Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and tolerance-based rank detection for a symmetric quadratic coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) have eigenpairs \((\lambda_i,u_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Its exact rank is \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=|\{i:\lambda_i\neq0\}|\). For a declared absolute tolerance \(\tau\geq0\), define \(I_\tau=\{i:|\lambda_i|>\tau\}\), the detected numerical rank \(r_\tau=|I_\tau|\), and the retained matrix \(Q_\tau=\sum_{i\in I_\tau}\lambda_i u_i u_i^T\). Eigenvalues satisfying \(|\lambda_i|\leq\tau\) are unresolved at that tolerance and are not thereby certified as exact zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rank counts nonzero eigenvalues. At a declared absolute tolerance, numerical rank counts eigenvalues whose magnitudes exceed the tolerance and retains precisely their eigenpairs; discarded eigenvalues are not certified as exact zeros.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\)
\(\tau\geq0\)
\((\lambda_i,u_i)\) are eigenpairs of \(Q\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=|\{i:\lambda_i\neq0\}|\), \(r_\tau=|\{i:|\lambda_i|>\tau\}|\), and \(Q_\tau=\sum_{i\in I_\tau}\lambda_i u_i u_i^T\).

notation.meaning: indices of eigenvalues retained at tolerance tau

children.title: Product–Rank Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationships between detected product patterns and low-rank lifted representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Product–Rank Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and inertia properties induced by products of linear forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\), the product \((a^Tx)(b^Tx)\) is represented under \(\tfrac12x^TQx\) by \(Q=ab^T+ba^T\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)\leq2\). If \(a\) and \(b\) are linearly independent, then \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=2\) and \(Q\) is indefinite on \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\). If \(b=\gamma a\) with \(a\neq0\) and \(\gamma\neq0\), then \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=1\). If either factor is zero, then \(Q=0\). Consequently, a sum of \(k\) products of linear forms has a symmetric quadratic matrix of rank at most \(2k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product of two linear forms has quadratic rank at most two. Independent nonzero factors give rank two and an indefinite matrix on their span; proportional nonzero factors give rank one, and a zero factor gives rank zero. A sum of k such products has rank at most 2k.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\)
\(Q=ab^T+ba^T\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)\leq2\); independent factors give rank two, proportional nonzero factors give rank one, and a sum of \(k\) product matrices has rank at most \(2k\).

notation.meaning: coefficient vectors of the two linear factors
nonzero proportionality scalar in the rank-one case

children.title: Quadratic Separability Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of independent scalar or block components in quadratic expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Separability Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive separability detected from the interaction graph of a symmetric quadratic matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx+d\) with \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), and partition the variable indices into nonempty sets \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\). The quadratic is additively separable across this partition if and only if \(Q_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i\in V_s\), \(j\in V_t\), and \(s\neq t\). Equivalently, a simultaneous permutation makes \(Q\) block diagonal. Then \(q(x)=d+\sum_{s=1}^k q_s(x_{V_s})\), assigning each linear coefficient to its unique block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic separates across variable blocks exactly when every cross-block matrix entry vanishes, equivalently when its matrix is block diagonal after permutation.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\)
\(\{V_1,\ldots,V_k\}\) partitions \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(x)=d+\sum_s q_s(x_{V_s})\iff Q_{V_sV_t}=0\text{ for all }s\neq t\).

children.title: Quadratic Sparsity Detection
children.top_down_role: Recognition of limited variable interactions in matrices, products, or interaction graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Sparsity Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural sparsity of a quadratic form through its matrix support and interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), define the exact quadratic interaction graph \(G(Q)=(V,E)\) by \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(E=\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j\leq n,\ Q_{ij}\neq0\}\). Define the diagonal support \(D=\{i:Q_{ii}\neq0\}\). The pair \((E,D)\) is the exact quadratic sparsity pattern. For a declared threshold \(\tau\geq0\), thresholded detection instead uses \(E_\tau=\{\{i,j\}:i<j,\ |Q_{ij}|>\tau\}\) and \(D_\tau=\{i:|Q_{ii}|>\tau\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact quadratic sparsity consists of the nonzero off-diagonal entries representing cross-products and the nonzero diagonal entries representing squares. With a declared threshold, only entries whose magnitudes exceed that threshold are detected.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\)
\(\tau\geq0\) when thresholded detection is used
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E=\{\{i,j\}:i<j,\ Q_{ij}\neq0\}\), \(D=\{i:Q_{ii}\neq0\}\), with thresholded analogues \(E_\tau\) and \(D_\tau\).

notation.meaning: supports detected at absolute threshold tau

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Block Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical decomposition induced by connected components of the quadratic interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx+d\) with \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) be the connected components of \(G(Q)\). There is a permutation matrix \(P\) such that \(P^TQP=\operatorname{diag}(Q_1,\ldots,Q_k)\), where \(Q_s=Q_{V_sV_s}\). Set \(z=P^Tx\) and partition \(P^Tc\) conformally as \((c_1,\ldots,c_k)\). Then \(q(x)=d+\sum_{s=1}^k(\tfrac12z_s^TQ_sz_s+c_s^Tz_s)\). The connected-component partition is the finest block decomposition determined solely by the nonzero off-diagonal quadratic interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The connected components of the quadratic interaction graph determine a permutation to block-diagonal form. After permuting the variables and linear coefficients conformally, the quadratic becomes a sum of independent block quadratics plus its constant term.
assumptions_latex: \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+c^Tx+d\)
\(Q\in\mathbb S^n\)
\(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) are the connected components of \(G(Q)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^TQP=\operatorname{diag}(Q_1,\ldots,Q_k)\) and \(q(x)=d+\sum_{s=1}^k(\tfrac12z_s^TQ_sz_s+c_s^Tz_s)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Native Quadratic versus Conic Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-order-cone lifting of a positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=R^TR\succeq0\). The native convex quadratic constraint \(x^TQx\leq t\) is equivalent to the rotated-cone system \((t,\tfrac12,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\), where \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,w):2uv\geq\|w\|_2^2,\ u\geq0,\ v\geq0\}\). Hence an MIQCP may retain the quadratic constraint or replace it by this conic constraint without changing its feasible mixed-integer points. The equivalence requires exact factorization and the positive-semidefinite curvature condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph can remain native or be represented exactly by a rotated second-order cone without changing feasible mixed-integer points.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=R^TR\succeq0\)
\(t\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^TQx\leq t\iff(t,\tfrac12,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Compact versus Lifted Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection equivalence between a compact quadratic model and an exact lifted formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\) and \(F=\{x\in X:q_j(x)\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\). Introduce lifted variables \(y=\phi(x)\) and functions \(\widetilde q_j\) satisfying \(\widetilde q_j(x,\phi(x))=q_j(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(j=1,\ldots,m\). The exact lifted set \(L=\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y=\phi(x),\ \widetilde q_j(x,y)\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_xL=F\). If \(y=\phi(x)\) is replaced by a relaxation whose feasible set contains its graph, the resulting projection contains \(F\) and may be strictly larger.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact product-linking constraints make the compact and lifted formulations projection-equivalent. Replacing the exact links by a relaxation produces a projection containing the compact feasible set and can weaken the formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\)
\(\widetilde q_j(x,\phi(x))=q_j(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(j=1,\ldots,m\)
\(y=\phi(x)\) is enforced exactly in \(L\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xL=F\); a lifted relaxation containing the exact graph has an \(x\)-projection containing \(F\).

knowledge_statements.title: Static versus Dynamic Convexification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of pre-generated relaxations with separation-driven refinement during mixed-integer search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X\), and let \(\{g_\alpha(x)\leq0:\alpha\in A\}\) be convex inequalities valid for \(F\). Static convexification chooses \(A_0\subseteq A\) before search and uses \(R_0=\{x\in X:g_\alpha(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }\alpha\in A_0\}\). Dynamic convexification constructs \(A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq A\), typically by separating relaxation solutions, and sets \(R_k=\{x\in X:g_\alpha(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }\alpha\in A_k\}\). Then \(F\subseteq R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\). If \(\bigcup_{k=0}^{\infty}A_k=A\), then \(\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}R_k=\{x\in X:g_\alpha(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }\alpha\in A\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Static convexification installs a selected valid family before search. Dynamic convexification adds valid inequalities over time, producing nested relaxations containing the feasible set. If every inequality in the full family is eventually included, the intersection of the relaxations equals the closure defined by that family.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq X\)
Each \(g_\alpha(x)\leq0\) is convex and valid for \(F\)
\(A_0\subseteq A_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq A\)
\(\bigcup_{k=0}^{\infty}A_k=A\) for the intersection equality
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\), and under exhaustive generation, \(\bigcap_{k=0}^{\infty}R_k=\{x\in X:g_\alpha(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }\alpha\in A\}\).

notation.meaning: full index set of valid convex inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral versus Semidefinite Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cut and positive-semidefinite relaxations of the rank-one quadratic lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Lift \(x x^T\) to \(X\in\mathbb S^n\). The exact relation is \(X=xx^T\), equivalently \(\begin{pmatrix}1&x^T\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\) together with rank one. Dropping rank gives the semidefinite route \(S=\{(x,X):\begin{pmatrix}1&x^T\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\}\). A polyhedral route replaces or outer-approximates this cone by finitely many linear inequalities \(a_k^Tx+\langle B_k,X\rangle\leq b_k\). Any such inequalities valid for \(S\) yield \(S\subseteq P\); adding separated valid inequalities tightens \(P\) toward the semidefinite relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The semidefinite route drops rank but keeps a PSD lift; the polyhedral route uses finitely many valid linear outer approximations of that cone.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\)
\(X\in\mathbb S^n\)
Every defining inequality of \(P\) is valid for \(S\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=xx^T\Rightarrow(x,X)\in S\subseteq P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Primal Heuristics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation-guided construction and local repair of feasible MIQCP incumbents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an MIQCP, a relaxation solution \(\bar x\), an incumbent value \(U\), and limits \(K,T\), generate at most \(K\) integer assignments \(z^k\) by rounding, diving, or randomized perturbation of the integer components of \(\bar x\). For each assignment, fix \(x_I=z^k\) and run a continuous quadratic or nonlinear local solver for at most \(T\) units to obtain \(x^k\). Accept \(x^k\) only if it satisfies all original constraints within the prescribed feasibility tolerance and improves \(U\). Stop after the limits are reached and return the best accepted incumbent, if any.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate integer assignments from a relaxation, repair each by continuous local optimization, and retain only solutions feasible for the original MIQCP that improve the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: A relaxation solution \(\bar x\) is available
Candidate feasibility is checked against the original constraints
\(K\) and \(T\) are finite limits
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathrm{out}}\) is either absent or is a checked feasible incumbent with objective value better than \(U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Cut Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pool-management rule for valid inequalities during quadratic branch-and-bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a node region \(X_v\), maintain a pool \(\mathcal C\) of inequalities \(a_i^\top x\le b_i\) valid for every feasible mixed-integer point. After solving the current relaxation at \(\bar x\), compute violations \(\nu_i=(a_i^\top\bar x-b_i)_+\) and scores \(s_i\) combining violation, efficacy, and numerical stability. Add a bounded subset of cuts with \(\nu_i>\varepsilon\), reoptimize, and increment the age of each inactive cut. Remove a cut only when its age exceeds a prescribed limit and retain globally valid cuts for descendant nodes. The resulting relaxation remains valid and its lower bound cannot decrease when cuts are added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add selected violated valid cuts, age inactive cuts, and delete stale ones. Adding cuts preserves all feasible points and cannot weaken a minimization lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X_v\) contains every feasible point compatible with node \(v\).
Every pool inequality is valid on the relevant feasible set.
Relaxations are solved as minimization problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing or Loose Product Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound dependence of McCormick relaxations for a bilinear product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w=xy\) with finite bounds \(\ell_x\le x\le u_x\) and \(\ell_y\le y\le u_y\). Its McCormick relaxation is the intersection of \(w\ge \ell_xy+\ell_yx-\ell_x\ell_y\), \(w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y\), \(w\le u_xy+\ell_yx-u_x\ell_y\), and \(w\le \ell_xy+u_yx-\ell_xu_y\). The maximum deviation of either envelope from \(xy\) equals \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\). Thus loose widths yield proportionally weak estimators, while a missing finite bound prevents this finite rectangular McCormick formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: McCormick error scales with the product of factor widths; absent finite bounds prevent the standard rectangular relaxation, and loose bounds weaken it.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are real variables.
The stated bounds are finite and ordered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The envelope deviation is \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\), so shrinking either factor interval strengthens the relaxation.

notation.meaning: lifted variable representing the product xy

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Indefinite Curvature Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-aware spectral classification of a symmetric quadratic Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric matrix \(Q\), choose absolute and relative tolerances \(\tau_a,\tau_r\ge0\) and set \(\tau=\tau_a+\tau_r\lVert Q\rVert_2\). Treat \(Q\) as numerically positive semidefinite at this tolerance when \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)\ge-\tau\). Within that tolerance-accepted region, label \(Q\) near-indefinite when \(-\tau\le\lambda_{\min}(Q)<0\); classify it as detectably indefinite when \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)<-\tau\). Near-indefinite status is a numerical-tolerance label and is not an exact positive-semidefiniteness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix whose smallest eigenvalue is negative but no smaller than the chosen scale-aware tolerance is a near-indefinite subtype of the matrices accepted numerically as positive semidefinite; more negative curvature is detectably indefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric.
\(\tau_a\) and \(\tau_r\) are declared nonnegative tolerances.
Eigenvalue and norm estimates use compatible numerical precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The predicate \(-\tau\le\lambda_{\min}(Q)<0\) defines the near-indefinite class at the selected tolerance without certifying \(Q\succeq0\) exactly.

children.title: Quadratic Scaling Pathologies

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Scaling Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient distortion induced by variable scaling in quadratic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x\) and diagonal scaling \(x=Dz\) with nonsingular \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\), the transformed data are \(Q'=D^\top QD\) and \(c'=D^\top c\). Hence \(Q'_{ij}=d_id_jQ_{ij}\). If the magnitudes \(|d_i|\) vary widely, initially comparable quadratic coefficients may acquire ratios proportional to \(|d_id_j|/|d_kd_l|\), causing overflow, underflow, cancellation, or tolerance-dependent constraint tests. Scaling is pathological when transformed coefficient ranges exceed the reliable dynamic range of the numerical method, even though the exact optimization problem is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal variable scaling multiplies each quadratic coefficient by two scale factors; extreme factors can create harmful coefficient ranges without changing the exact model.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric.
Every diagonal entry of \(D\) is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact equivalence under \(x=Dz\) does not imply numerically equivalent coefficient magnitudes or residual tests.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling identities are correct and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the asserted numerical consequences and the boundary based on a method's reliable dynamic range require an authoritative numerical-scaling source.

children.title: Quadratic Conditioning Pathologies

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Conditioning Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral criterion for ill-conditioned quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be symmetric and nonsingular, with singular values \(\sigma_{\max}(Q)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_{\min}(Q)>0\). Its spectral condition number is \(\kappa_2(Q)=\sigma_{\max}(Q)/\sigma_{\min}(Q)\). For a declared relative resolution \(\eta>0\), call the quadratic curvature numerically ill-conditioned when \(\sigma_{\min}(Q)\le\eta\sigma_{\max}(Q)\), equivalently \(\kappa_2(Q)\ge1/\eta\). In this regime, relative perturbations of size comparable to \(\eta\) can substantially alter computed stationary points, curvature classifications, or linear-system solves involving \(Q\); singular \(Q\) has infinite condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic curvature is ill-conditioned when its smallest singular value is below the declared relative resolution times its largest singular value.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric.
Conditioning is measured in the matrix two-norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pathology predicate is \(\sigma_{\min}(Q)\le\eta\sigma_{\max}(Q)\), with \(\kappa_2(Q)=\infty\) when \(Q\) is singular.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition-number definition and threshold equivalence are correct. The broader claims about stationary points, curvature classifications, and solver behavior require a conditioning or perturbation-analysis source.

children.title: Scaling–Conditioning Interaction

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling–Conditioning Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of diagonal congruence scaling on inertia and conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nonsingular diagonal change of variables \(x=Dz\), a symmetric quadratic matrix becomes \(Q'=D^\top QD\). Sylvester's law of inertia gives \(\operatorname{inertia}(Q')=\operatorname{inertia}(Q)\), so exact convexity or indefiniteness is unchanged. Spectral conditioning is not invariant: \(\kappa_2(Q')\le\kappa_2(D)^2\kappa_2(Q)\) when \(Q\) is nonsingular, while the reverse comparison follows by applying the same inequality with \(D^{-1}\). Consequently, scaling can improve or degrade numerical conditioning even though it preserves the exact signs of curvature directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular diagonal scaling preserves the numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues, but it may improve or worsen spectral conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric and nonsingular.
\(D\) is a nonsingular diagonal matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{inertia}(D^\top QD)=\operatorname{inertia}(Q)\), but generally \(\kappa_2(D^\top QD)\ne\kappa_2(Q)\).

notation.meaning: counts of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Lifting Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size growth from explicitly lifting all quadratic monomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), a full symmetric lifting introduces one variable \(W_{ij}\) for every monomial \(x_ix_j\) with \(1\le i\le j\le n\). Therefore the lift contains \(n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)\) additional scalar variables. If every lifted entry receives a constant positive number of envelope or linking inequalities, their number is also \(\Theta(n^2)\). A matrix-based semidefinite lifting likewise represents a dense symmetric matrix \(W\) of order \(n\), requiring \(\Theta(n^2)\) scalar entries before accounting for semidefinite factorization costs. Sparsity-restricted lifting reduces this count by introducing entries only for selected monomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifting every distinct quadratic monomial adds exactly n(n+1)/2 scalar variables, while dense matrix-based liftings and constant-per-entry linking systems have quadratic size.
assumptions_latex: All distinct monomials \(x_ix_j\) with \(1\le i\le j\le n\) are lifted.
The lifted matrix is represented symmetrically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scalar storage and formulation-size growth of a dense quadratic lift is \(\Theta(n^2)\).

notation.meaning: lifted representative of the monomial x_i x_j

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Partition Localization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of spatial branching to shrink the intervals controlling relaxation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bilinear term \(xy\) on a partition cell \([\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\), the deviation of either McCormick envelope from \(xy\) is at most \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/4\). A partition is weakly localized for this term when descendant cells do not substantially reduce either factor width. In particular, branching only on variables absent from the term leaves its McCormick relaxation unchanged. Convergence of this local envelope error to zero requires that along every retained infinite branch, at least one factor width for each unresolved bilinear term tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partitioning is weak when it fails to shrink variables in unresolved products; branching on unrelated variables leaves the product relaxation unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Each bilinear term has finite rectangular bounds.
McCormick envelopes are recomputed on every partition cell.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If neither factor width shrinks, the termwise envelope-error bound need not converge to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Native MIQCP Architectures

A native MIQCP architecture drops integrality at each node and solves the resulting convex QCP, or an equivalent conic formulation, to obtain a lower bound. With finite integer domains and certified node solves, exhaustive processing returns a global optimum or proves infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Native Architecture Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical selection rule for native MIQP versus MIQCP processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mixed-integer quadratic model, select native convex MIQP processing when all nonlinearities occur in a convex quadratic objective and the remaining constraints are linear. Select native convex MIQCP processing when one or more constraints have convex quadratic form \(g_j(x)\le0\), optionally after an exact second-order-cone representation. These selections provide valid convex node relaxations only under the corresponding curvature conditions. If a minimized quadratic objective or a sublevel quadratic constraint is nonconvex on its node domain, convex-native processing alone does not certify a global lower bound; a valid global relaxation, spatial branching, or an exact reformulation is additionally required.

Quadratic matrices are interpreted through their symmetric parts.
Architecture selection must support global certification.

knowledge_statements.title: MILP-Based Quadratic Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial MILP reformulation for bounded nonconvex mixed-integer quadratic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bounded mixed-integer quadratic model, introduce one variable \(w_{ij}\) for each product \(x_i x_j\). On the current variable box, replace every identity \(w_{ij}=x_i x_j\) by valid polyhedral under- and overestimators, producing an MILP relaxation. Solve this relaxation to obtain a lower bound \(L\); evaluate or locally improve feasible candidates to obtain an incumbent value \(U\). If \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\), return the incumbent. Otherwise branch on an integer variable or subdivide the domain of a continuous factor, rebuild the affected envelopes, and repeat. With finite factor bounds and exhaustive refinement, the relaxation error vanishes and the retained incumbent converges to a global optimum.

The MILP subproblems are solved globally.

knowledge_statements.title: Global MINLP Quadratic Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic spatial branch-and-bound for nonconvex quadratic MINLPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded mixed-integer nonlinear program containing nonconvex quadratic terms, initialize an active list with the original mixed-integer domain and set the incumbent value to \(U=+\infty\). For each active node, construct a convex relaxation using valid convex underestimators of the quadratic terms and solve it globally to obtain a node lower bound. Fathom an infeasible node or any node whose bound is at least \(U-\varepsilon\). From relaxation or local-search points, retain every feasible solution improving \(U\). Otherwise branch on an unfixed integer variable or spatially partition a bounded continuous variable. Return the incumbent when the minimum active-node bound \(L\) satisfies \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\).
